To explore this concept thoroughly, we can break down how these seemingly disparate elements—lyric poetry, literary sublimity, and apocalyptic theology—connect. The Core Entities & The Transmission Chain Sappho's Fragment 31: Arguably the most famous ancient poem about desire. It details a psychosomatic crisis: the speaker sees the beloved, her tongue breaks, fire runs under her skin, her eyes go blind, her ears ring, and she feels "only a little short of dying." It is a fragmentation of the self caused by the overwhelming presence of the divine/beloved. Longinus (On the Sublime): Writing centuries later, the anonymous author known as Longinus uses Sappho's Fragment 31 as the ultimate example of the Sublime (hypsos). He praises how Sappho takes agonizing, disparate physical symptoms and binds them together into a unified whole. Longinus is the one who preserved Fragment 31 for history; without his treatise, the poem would be largely lost. The Logos: Historically attributed to Heraclitus, the Stoics, and later Philo of Alexandria before being Christianized in the Gospel of John ("In the beginning was the Word/Logos"). It represents cosmic order, reason, and the speech of God. The Apocalypse (Revelation): The ultimate biblical text of trauma, cosmic fragmentation, unsealing, and divine presence, culminating in the Alpha and the Omega (Ω). He shows how human language can stretch, break, and reconstruct itself to handle things that are beyond human endurance. ⚡ From Eros to Logos The traditional narrative says the Logos is purely rational, masculine, and philosophical. Your thesis introduces an "erratum" (a corrected historical mistake): the Logos actually inherits its power from the ecstatic, overwhelming physical truth found in Sappho. Sappho's poetry is about the terror and beauty of a localized epiphany (the beloved sitting like a god). It is a macrocosmic version of the somatic breakdown Sappho describes in her micro-cosmos of desire. The Omega (Ω): The ultimate end, the final letter, the collapse of time.
